questions.stem: In the Roman Republic of Caesar's time, the highest regular magistracy was held by:
options: two consuls, elected each year to serve together
one king, chosen for life by the senate and people
ten tribunes, appointed by the senate every five years
a single dictator, elected each year by the assemblies
questions.explanation: Power was divided among annually elected magistrates who served with colleagues, so no one man held supreme authority for long. A dictator was appointed only in emergencies and traditionally for six months at most, which is why Caesar's long dictatorships broke with custom.

questions.stem: The cursus honorum was the sequence of offices in a Roman political career. Which order matches Caesar's career?
options: praetor, quaestor, aedile, consul
quaestor, praetor, consul, aedile
quaestor, aedile, praetor, consul
aedile, quaestor, consul, praetor
questions.explanation: Caesar was quaestor in 69, curule aedile in 65, praetor in 62 and consul in 59 BCE. Unlike Pompey, he rose through the offices in the normal order.

questions.stem: In 69 BCE, at the funeral of his aunt Julia, Caesar claimed that his family descended from kings and, through Iulus son of Aeneas, from the goddess Venus. His main purpose was to:
options: prove that the Julii had been the first family to hold the consulship
build his own prestige on the ancient status of the patrician Julii
show that the Julii had always been plebeians who opposed the senate
argue that Rome should restore the monarchy with himself as its king
questions.explanation: Suetonius preserves the claim of royal and divine ancestry from this speech. The Julii were an old patrician family that had produced few recent consuls, so Caesar used their legendary past to win attention and standing.

questions.stem: Caesar's aunt Julia was the widow of Marius, and his first wife, Cornelia, was the daughter of Cinna. How did these family links affect his early career?
options: They forced him to join the optimates and defend senatorial power
They made him a plebeian, so he could stand for election as tribune
They tied him to Sulla's enemies, so he was in danger after Sulla won
They made him a favourite of Sulla, who appointed him to the senate at once
questions.explanation: Caesar refused Sulla's order to divorce Cornelia and had to go into hiding before he was pardoned. Suetonius reports Sulla's warning that 'in this Caesar there is more than one Marius'.

questions.stem: Plutarch and Suetonius both tell how the young Caesar, captured by pirates, joked that he would have them executed and later did so. A historian evaluating the story should note that:
options: it comes from Caesar's Commentaries, so it is an eyewitness account
it was invented by Cicero, who hated Caesar and wanted to shame him publicly
both writers were present and saw the events with their own eyes
it was told long afterwards and later writers may have embellished it
questions.explanation: Both biographers wrote well over a century later, and an anecdote that so neatly shows Caesar's confidence and ruthlessness may have grown in the telling. Agreement between them may simply mean they drew on the same earlier source.

questions.stem: As curule aedile in 65 BCE, Caesar staged lavish games and restored the trophies of Marius. Which method of gaining power does this show?
options: winning the support of the senate by cutting public spending on festivals
gaining a military command by recruiting soldiers from the Roman crowd
gaining religious authority by holding new games in honour of the war god Mars
winning popular favour by spending heavily, even at the cost of large debts
questions.explanation: Caesar borrowed heavily to fund spectacular games and openly honoured Marius, appealing to the people and to Marius's old supporters. His debts were so large that his political success became essential to his survival.

questions.stem: In the senate debate of December 63 BCE on the arrested Catilinarian conspirators, Caesar:
options: argued that they should be imprisoned and their property seized rather than executed
argued that they should be executed at once without any trial, as Cato also wanted
argued that they should be released, as he had secretly led the conspiracy himself
argued that the matter should be handed to Pompey, who was still in the East
questions.explanation: Sallust's account presents Caesar's speech against the death penalty and Cato's reply demanding execution, which carried the senate. Rumours linked Caesar to Catiline, but no evidence shows he led the plot.

questions.stem: After the Bona Dea scandal of 62 BCE, Plutarch reports that Caesar divorced his wife Pompeia because:
options: his wife ought not even to be under suspicion
she had been convicted of sacrilege in court
Sulla had ordered him to marry Pompey's daughter
she had refused to move to his province in Spain
questions.explanation: Clodius had entered Caesar's house during the women-only rites of the Bona Dea. Asked why he divorced Pompeia, Caesar said he thought his wife ought not even to be under suspicion, protecting his own standing as pontifex maximus.

questions.stem: Which pairing correctly shows what one member of the First Triumvirate wanted from the alliance?
options: Pompey: a five-year command against the Parthian empire in Syria
Crassus: land in Campania for the veterans of his eastern campaigns
Pompey: the consulship of 59 BCE and a five-year command in Gaul and Illyricum
Crassus: relief for the tax-farming companies holding the Asian contract
questions.explanation: Crassus wanted the Asian tax contract reduced for his equestrian allies, Pompey wanted land for his veterans and ratification of his eastern settlement, and Caesar wanted the consulship and a major provincial command. Crassus's Parthian command came later, in 55 BCE.

questions.stem: Suetonius says that wits dated documents of 59 BCE 'in the consulship of Julius and Caesar'. The joke reflects the fact that:
options: the people elected Caesar twice because of an error in the voting
the senate refused to recognise either of the elected consuls
Caesar's colleague Bibulus had withdrawn and Caesar dominated the year
Caesar held both consulships at once after his colleague was killed in a riot
questions.explanation: After being driven from the Forum, Bibulus stayed at home announcing unfavourable omens, so Caesar governed as if he were sole consul. The joke is gossip recorded by Suetonius, but it captures how contemporaries saw the year.

questions.stem: The lex Vatinia of 59 BCE gave Caesar, for five years, the provinces of:
options: Further Spain and Lusitania
Syria and Cilicia
Macedonia and Achaea
Cisalpine Gaul and Illyricum
questions.explanation: The tribune Vatinius passed the law giving Caesar Cisalpine Gaul and Illyricum, and the senate added Transalpine Gaul. These provinces became the base for his conquest of Gaul.

questions.stem: At the conference at Luca in 56 BCE, the three allies renewed their alliance. As a result:
options: Caesar became sole consul for 55 and Pompey took over the command of Gaul instead
Crassus retired from politics and divided his fortune between the others
Pompey married Caesar's daughter Julia and Caesar married Pompey's sister
Pompey and Crassus became consuls for 55 and Caesar's command was extended
questions.explanation: The renewal gave Pompey and Crassus a second joint consulship in 55 BCE, and their law extended Caesar's Gallic command by five years. Pompey had already married Julia in 59 BCE.

questions.stem: Caesar's conquest of Gaul reached its climax in 52 BCE when he defeated the revolt led by:
options: Cassivellaunus, in southern Britain
Pharnaces, at the battle of Zela
Vercingetorix, at the siege of Alesia
Ariovistus, on the banks of the Rhine
questions.explanation: Vercingetorix united much of Gaul against Rome but surrendered after Caesar's siege of Alesia. Ariovistus was defeated in 58 BCE, and Pharnaces was the king of Pontus beaten at Zela in 47 BCE.

questions.stem: Caesar crossed the Rhine in 55 BCE and led expeditions to Britain in 55 and 54 BCE, but conquered neither region. The most likely reason for these campaigns is that they:
options: allowed Caesar to avoid returning to Rome when his consulship ended in 59 BCE
brought enormous prestige in Rome, where the senate decreed long thanksgivings
were ordered by the senate, which wanted Britain's tin mines for the treasury
were needed to rescue Crassus, who was trapped by the Germans across the Rhine
questions.explanation: Crossing the Ocean to Britain and bridging the Rhine were spectacular feats that impressed opinion at Rome and kept Caesar in the public eye. Crassus died in 53 BCE fighting the Parthians, not the Germans.

questions.stem: Caesar wrote seven books of Commentaries on the Gallic War. The eighth book, covering the last years in Gaul, was written by:
options: Gaius Sallustius
Aulus Hirtius
Asinius Pollio
Titus Labienus
questions.explanation: Hirtius, one of Caesar's officers, completed the work after Caesar's death. Labienus was Caesar's leading general in Gaul who later joined Pompey, and Pollio wrote a separate history of the civil wars.

questions.stem: Cicero praised Caesar's Commentaries as bare and unadorned, stripped of ornament like a garment removed, and said Caesar meant them as material for later historians. Why does this plain style call for caution?
options: It shows the Commentaries were really written by Cicero rather than by Caesar himself
It proves Caesar never took part in the campaigns he describes
It means the Commentaries contain no information about events
It gives an impression of objectivity to an account written to serve Caesar
questions.explanation: Writing simply, in the third person, makes Caesar's version of events seem factual, while he chose what to include and how to justify each war. The Commentaries are an eyewitness account by the commander, but also political self-presentation.

questions.stem: In January 49 BCE the tribunes Mark Antony and Quintus Cassius fled from Rome to Caesar after the senate overrode their veto. In his Civil War commentary, Caesar used this to:
options: prove that the senate had already declared him dictator for life
explain why he gave up his army before he returned to Italy
show that Pompey had crossed the Rubicon into Caesar's province first
claim he was defending his dignity and the rights of the tribunes
questions.explanation: Caesar presented his invasion of Italy as protecting his dignitas and the sacred rights of the tribunes. This is self-justification: his opponents saw it as an attack on the Republic by a governor who refused to give up his army.

questions.stem: Plutarch says Asinius Pollio was among Caesar's friends at the Rubicon, where Caesar said 'Let the die be cast'. Pollio later wrote a history of the civil wars that is now lost. How does this affect the reliability of Plutarch's account?
options: It may rest on an eyewitness, though one who served on Caesar's side
It must be fiction, because no one at all was with Caesar at the river
It is official record, because Pollio wrote it for the senate
It is neutral, because Pollio fought for Pompey at Pharsalus
questions.explanation: If Plutarch drew on Pollio, the scene may go back to someone who was present. Pollio was a Caesarian officer, though, so his account might shape the moment to show Caesar's hesitation and resolve.

questions.stem: At Corfinium in 49 BCE Caesar released Domitius Ahenobarbus and other captured opponents unharmed. This policy of clementia was intended mainly to:
options: win over moderates by contrast with Sulla's proscriptions
punish the senate by sending its leaders into exile
obey an old law that banned the execution of Roman senators
persuade Pompey to give up command of his legions
questions.explanation: Caesar's mercy encouraged neutrals and opponents to accept his victory, in sharp contrast to Sulla's killings. Some critics saw clemency itself as a kingly act, since only a master can pardon.

questions.stem: Caesar decisively defeated Pompey in 48 BCE at the battle of:
options: Pharsalus
Thapsus
Munda
Philippi
questions.explanation: At Pharsalus in Greece Caesar defeated Pompey, who fled to Egypt and was killed there. Thapsus (46 BCE) and Munda (45 BCE) were later battles against the Pompeians, and Philippi (42 BCE) came after Caesar's death.

questions.stem: Suetonius says 'I came, I saw, I conquered' was displayed in Caesar's Pontic triumph, while Plutarch says Caesar wrote the three words to his friend Amantius in Rome. What is the best conclusion?
options: The sources contradict each other, so Caesar can never have used the phrase
Plutarch must be correct because he wrote before Suetonius and used Caesar's letters
Suetonius must be correct because he worked in the imperial archives
The sources differ in detail but agree Caesar used the phrase to stress his speed
questions.explanation: The two accounts are compatible: the phrase could have appeared in a letter and on a placard. Both show Caesar advertising the speed of his victory over Pharnaces at Zela in 47 BCE.

questions.stem: After Caesar's victory at Thapsus in 46 BCE, Cato took his own life at Utica. His death mattered because it:
options: allowed Caesar to seize Cato's legions and invade Egypt
showed that Cato had secretly supported Caesar all along
made him a martyr for the Republic who had refused Caesar's pardon
left Caesar without any enemies, so the civil war ended at once in Africa
questions.explanation: By choosing death rather than owe his life to Caesar's clemency, Cato became a symbol of republican liberty for later opponents of one-man rule. The war continued until Munda in 45 BCE.

questions.stem: Plutarch, describing Caesar's appointment as dictator for life early in 44 BCE, says 'This was confessedly a tyranny'. In context, his judgment rests on the fact that:
options: the senate had refused to vote for the appointment and was dissolved
Caesar had taken the title of king in a ceremony at the Lupercalia
the office removed the time limit that had defined the dictatorship
Caesar had abolished the consulship and the popular assemblies
questions.explanation: Traditional dictators served briefly in emergencies; a lifelong dictatorship meant permanent supremacy. The consulship and assemblies continued, and Caesar publicly refused the diadem at the Lupercalia.

questions.stem: Caesar's calendar reform, which took effect from 1 January 45 BCE, introduced:
options: a lunar year of 354 days with an extra month every second year
a year of ten months beginning in March, as in Romulus's time
a year of 360 days divided into twelve equal months of 30 days
a year of 365 days with an extra day every fourth year
questions.explanation: Advised by the astronomer Sosigenes of Alexandria, Caesar replaced the irregular republican calendar with a solar year of 365 days plus a leap day. The Julian calendar remained the basis of the modern calendar.

questions.stem: Suetonius says Caesar cut the number of citizens receiving free grain in Rome from 320,000 to 150,000. By how many did the number fall?
questions.explanation: 320,000 minus 150,000 is 170,000, more than half of the original number. Suetonius also reports that Caesar sent 80,000 citizens to colonies overseas, which helped relieve pressure on the city.

questions.stem: Caesar enlarged the senate to about 900 members, adding many of his supporters, including some from the provinces. Critics most likely saw this as:
options: cheapening the senate and filling it with men loyal to him
a return to the senate's size in the early days of the Republic
a step that gave the senate control over Caesar's armies
a way to remove all patricians from the senate for good
questions.explanation: Expanding the senate rewarded followers and gave Caesar a body full of his own men, which offended traditional senators. The enlargement made the senate less independent, not more powerful.

questions.stem: Denarii minted in 44 BCE show Caesar's portrait with the legend CAESAR DICT PERPETVO (Caesar, dictator for life). Why are these coins significant evidence?
options: No living Roman had appeared on coins of the city before, a sign of quasi-royal status
They prove the senate had crowned Caesar king of Rome before the Ides of March
They show that Caesar refused all honours and wanted only the title of consul
They were minted by the conspirators to justify the assassination of a tyrant
questions.explanation: Placing a living man's head on Roman coins broke with republican custom and resembled the coinage of Hellenistic kings. Official coins show how Caesar's power was presented, which is different from how all Romans received it.

questions.stem: At the Lupercalia on 15 February 44 BCE, Antony offered Caesar a diadem, which Caesar refused. Weeks earlier, Suetonius says, he had answered people hailing him as king, 'I am Caesar and no king'. Why do historians interpret the episode differently?
options: No ancient writer mentions the Lupercalia, so the story is modern
Cleopatra's letters say the diadem was a gift she sent from Egypt
The sources do not reveal whether it was staged or a genuine test of opinion
The ancient sources disagree about whether Caesar accepted or refused the diadem
questions.explanation: The sources agree he refused, but not on his motive: he may have been rejecting monarchy publicly, testing the crowd, or playing out a staged scene. Motives are hard to prove from accounts written long after the event.

questions.stem: According to Suetonius, how many men joined the conspiracy against Caesar?
options: exactly twelve
about three hundred
only Brutus and Cassius
more than sixty
questions.explanation: Suetonius says more than sixty joined the plot, led by Gaius Cassius and Marcus and Decimus Brutus. Several conspirators, including Marcus Brutus, had been pardoned and promoted by Caesar.

questions.stem: Shakespeare made the line 'Et tu, Brute?' famous. What does Suetonius actually report about Caesar's last words?
options: He made a long speech defending his dictatorship before he fell
He died silent, though some said he asked Brutus in Greek, 'You too, my child?'
He shouted 'Et tu, Brute?' in Latin, as all of the eyewitnesses later agreed in court
He cursed the senate and named Antony as the man who betrayed him
questions.explanation: Suetonius says Caesar uttered no word beyond a groan, though some writers reported the Greek words to Brutus. The Latin line comes from the later dramatic tradition, not from the ancient sources.

questions.stem: Brutus later issued a coin showing a cap of liberty between two daggers with the words EID MAR (the Ides of March). The coin shows that the conspirators:
options: wanted to make Brutus king in place of Julius Caesar
presented the killing as freeing Rome from tyranny
regretted the murder and asked the gods for pardon
blamed Antony for planning and carrying out the attack
questions.explanation: The cap of liberty was worn by freed slaves, so the design claims that Caesar's death restored freedom to the Roman people. It is propaganda from the conspirators' side, just as Caesar's coins promoted his own position.

questions.stem: In letters to Atticus in 44 BCE, Cicero complained that the conspirators had shown the courage of men but the judgment of boys: the tree had been cut down, not uprooted. He meant that they had:
options: spared Caesar's life when they should have exiled him from Rome
killed Caesar but left his supporters and his system of power in place
uprooted the Republic itself by murdering its lawful elected consul
acted too slowly, allowing Caesar to leave Rome for his planned Parthian war
questions.explanation: Antony and Caesar's other followers kept their positions and the dictator's arrangements stayed in force, so the assassination did not restore the old Republic. Cicero's letter is private and candid, unlike his public speeches.

questions.stem: Which of these was a consequence of Caesar's will, read after his death?
options: Caesarion was named king of Egypt and heir to his whole estate
his gardens and wealth were left to the conspirators
Gaius Octavius was named heir to three-quarters of his estate
Mark Antony was adopted as his son and heir to his name
questions.explanation: Suetonius says the will made Octavius heir to three-quarters of the estate and left each citizen 300 sesterces and his gardens near the Tiber for public use. The generosity of the will helped turn the people against the conspirators.

questions.stem: Suetonius, author of the Life of the Deified Julius, had worked as a secretary to the emperor Hadrian. What is the main strength and weakness of his biography?
options: He used only Caesar's Commentaries, but he translated them into Greek
He may have used archive material, but he includes gossip and arranges by topic
He was an eyewitness to Caesar's career, but he wrote only in praise of the dictator
He wrote a year-by-year narrative, but he left out Caesar's private life
questions.explanation: Suetonius had access to imperial records and quotes documents, but he groups material under headings such as appearance and habits and repeats rumour freely. He wrote in the second century CE, long after Caesar's death.

questions.stem: Plutarch paired his Life of Caesar with a Life of Alexander the Great. This tells us that Plutarch was mainly interested in:
options: character and moral lessons drawn from great men's lives
a precise military record of every battle in Caesar's wars
the economic causes of the fall of the Roman Republic
defending the Roman Republic against Greek critics
questions.explanation: Plutarch's Parallel Lives compare a Greek and a Roman to explore virtue and vice, so he selects anecdotes that reveal character. A historian must allow for this moral purpose when using his details.

questions.stem: Appian and Cassius Dio wrote narratives of Caesar's career in Greek, in the second and third centuries CE. Their perspective is shaped most by the fact that they:
options: had served as officers under Caesar and wished to defend his reputation
were Gauls who blamed Caesar for the conquest of their own homeland
had no Roman sources and relied entirely on Gallic oral traditions
lived under emperors and saw Caesar as a stage on the road to monarchy
questions.explanation: Writing long after the Republic had become an empire, both read Caesar's career knowing what followed. Dio, a senator and consul, was also interested in how one man came to hold supreme power.

questions.stem: In 46 BCE Cicero praised Caesar's clemency in a speech thanking him for pardoning Marcellus; after the Ides he treated Caesar as a tyrant whose death was justified. What does this suggest about using Cicero as a source?
options: His speeches are always more reliable than his letters because they were public
He had no direct knowledge of Caesar, so his opinions are worthless as evidence
He was a consistent supporter of Caesar, so his later criticism must be a forgery
His views depend on audience and circumstances, so each work must be read in context
questions.explanation: Cicero was a contemporary who knew Caesar well, but his public speeches were shaped by what he needed to achieve at the time. Comparing his speeches with his more candid letters helps reveal his real attitudes.

questions.stem: Theodor Mommsen in the nineteenth century portrayed Caesar as a statesman of genius who rescued Rome from a decayed oligarchy. Erich Gruen (1974) argued the Republic was not doomed before the civil war. How does Gruen's view challenge Mommsen's?
options: It argues that Caesar was a poor general who lost most of his battles
It claims Caesar never held the dictatorship or reformed the calendar
It agrees with Mommsen but adds new evidence from the Commentaries
It denies that the Republic was so decayed that a saviour was needed
questions.explanation: Mommsen's admiring picture assumes the Republic had failed and Caesar was its necessary replacement. Gruen argued republican institutions still worked in the 50s BCE and that the civil war itself destroyed them, which makes Caesar's role look less inevitable.

questions.stem: Caesar's family name later became a title of rulers, as in the German Kaiser and the Russian Tsar. This shows that:
options: his name came to stand for supreme personal power long after his death
he was the first Roman since Tarquin to take the formal title of king of Rome
Augustus banned the name to stop anyone from imitating Caesar
every emperor after him was a blood descendant of the Julii
questions.explanation: Because Augustus and his successors took the name Caesar, it became a title for emperors and later for monarchs. Caesar himself refused the title of king, and later emperors were often not related to him.

questions.stem: Augustus held power for over forty years, while Caesar was killed within weeks of becoming dictator for life. Which judgment of Caesar's long-term significance is best supported?
options: He was quickly forgotten, and his reforms were all reversed after the Ides of March
He left no heir, so the empire was divided among his officers after his death
He showed that one-man rule could take over Rome, but his heir learned to disguise it
He restored the Republic, which survived unchanged until the reign of Constantine
questions.explanation: Caesar's dictatorship ended collective republican government, but open monarchy provoked his murder. Octavian avoided the dictatorship and the title of king while holding real power, and Caesar's calendar and colonies outlasted him.
